lessons.title: C++ Syntax
lessons.introduction: Syntax is the grammar of C++: semicolons, curly braces, parentheses, and exact spelling that allow the compiler to understand your intent.
objectives: Identify the purpose of semicolons (;), curly braces ({ }), and parentheses ( ).
Spot and fix common C++ syntax errors before uploading.
Understand case sensitivity in C++ identifiers.
conceptExplanation: Just as English uses periods and punctuation to separate sentences, C++ uses strict symbols. A missing semicolon or unmatched brace prevents compilation.
The compiler is your friend, not your enemy: when it reports a syntax error, it tells you the exact line where grammar broke.
lessons.analogy: Syntax is like punctuation in a contract — missing one mark can completely change the meaning or make it invalid.

syntaxExplanation.summary: Blocks use { }, function calls use ( ), and statements end with ;.
rules: Every opening { must have a matching closing }.
Every opening ( must have a matching closing ).
C++ is strictly case-sensitive.

codeExamples.title: Clean C++ Syntax Structure
codeExamples.description: A valid minimal sketch showing matched braces, parentheses, and semicolons.

lineByLine.explanation: Function signature with () and opening block brace {.
Function call with argument 9600 ending in semicolon ;.
Closes the setup() block cleanly.

lessons.realWorldApplication: Every Arduino library and robotics firmware file relies on strict C++ syntax to compile cleanly across different microcontrollers.

commonMistakes.mistake: Forgetting a closing brace }
commonMistakes.fix: Use Arduino IDE's Auto Format (Ctrl+T / Cmd+T) to spot mismatched braces instantly.

commonMistakes.mistake: Using smart/curly quotes instead of straight quotes
commonMistakes.fix: Always use standard straight double quotes " " for strings.

options: Missing semicolon at the end of pinMode(13, OUTPUT)
exercises.explanation: Statements in C++ must end with a semicolon (;).

exercises.prompt: Are ledPin and LEDPIN considered the same variable in C++?
exercises.explanation: C++ treats uppercase and lowercase letters as distinct characters.

summary: Statements end with semicolons (;); blocks are enclosed in braces ({ }).
C++ is case-sensitive.
Use Arduino IDE Auto Format (Ctrl+T) to keep braces aligned.

lessons.title: Statements
lessons.introduction: A statement is a single complete instruction executed by the microcontroller.
objectives: Recognize declaration, assignment, and function-call statements.
Understand compound statements (blocks) enclosed in curly braces.
Trace multi-statement execution accurately.
conceptExplanation: Programs are built out of statements. A declaration statement introduces a variable, an assignment statement updates a value, and a function-call statement tells hardware or helper code to perform an action.
Multiple statements grouped inside { } form a compound statement (block), which lets if statements, loops, and functions execute several instructions together.
lessons.analogy: Each statement is a single sentence in an instruction manual; a block { } is a paragraph.

syntaxExplanation.summary: One statement per line keeps code clear and easy to debug.
syntaxExplanation.pattern:
int count = 0;        // Declaration statement
count = count + 1;    // Assignment statement
Serial.println(count);// Function-call statement
rules: End simple statements with ;
Do not put a semicolon right after if (...) or void setup().

codeExamples.title: Three Statement Types in Action
codeExamples.description: Shows declaration, assignment, and function call statements working together.

lineByLine.explanation: Declaration + initialization statement.
Assignment statement updating speed to 75.
Function-call statement printing 75.

lessons.realWorldApplication: Sensor calibration routines execute ordered assignment statements to subtract zero-offset errors before driving actuators.

commonMistakes.mistake: Placing a semicolon right after if (x > 5);
commonMistakes.fix: An extra semicolon creates an empty statement, detaching the { } block from the if condition!

commonMistakes.mistake: Cramming 5 statements onto one line
commonMistakes.fix: Write one statement per line for readability.

tryItYourself.title: m03_statements.ino
tryItYourself.challengePrompt: Add a statement that multiplies speed by 2 before printing.
tryItYourself.expectedBehavior: Multiplying speed by 2 prints 150 to the Serial Monitor.

exercises.prompt: Why does this LED always turn on even when x is 0?
options: The stray semicolon after if (x > 10); terminates the if early.
exercises.explanation: A semicolon directly after if (...) creates an empty statement, so the following { } block runs unconditionally.

exercises.prompt: Complete the assignment statement to increase score by 10.
exercises.explanation: score = score + 10; adds 10 to the current value and stores the result back in score.

summary: Statements are individual executable instructions ending in ';'.
Braces { } group statements into blocks.
Never place a stray semicolon immediately after an if() header.

lessons.title: Comments
lessons.introduction: Comments let you explain WHY your code exists, document wiring connections, and temporarily disable lines during debugging.
objectives: Write single-line (//) and multi-line (/* ... */) comments.
Explain why good comments describe intent and wiring rather than restating obvious syntax.
Use comments safely to isolate lines while debugging.
conceptExplanation: C++ supports two comment styles: // comments out the rest of a single line, while /* ... */ comments out multiple lines.
Write comments that help your future self: pin wiring notes, physical units (cm, ms, mV), and why a specific threshold was chosen.
lessons.analogy: Comments are sticky notes attached to a blueprint — they guide engineers without altering the final machine.

syntaxExplanation.summary: Core C++ syntax pattern for Comments:
rules: Comments are removed by the compiler and use 0 bytes of Flash or SRAM.
Never nest /* /* ... */ */ multi-line comments.

codeExamples.title: Documenting Wiring & Units with Comments
codeExamples.description: Shows effective engineering comments on an ultrasonic sensor pin map.

lineByLine.explanation: Multi-line header documenting board voltage and wiring.
Inline comment specifying exact physical timing.

lessons.realWorldApplication: Clear wiring comments at the top of a sketch let you rebuild the breadboard circuit months later without guessing.

commonMistakes.mistake: Writing useless comments like 'i++; // add 1 to i'
commonMistakes.fix: Explain WHY, units, or wiring instead of repeating obvious C++ syntax.

commonMistakes.mistake: Forgetting to close a /* multi-line comment
commonMistakes.fix: Every /* must have a matching */ or the compiler ignores the rest of your file.

tryItYourself.title: m03_comments.ino
tryItYourself.challengePrompt: Add a single-line comment explaining what baud rate 9600 means.
tryItYourself.expectedBehavior: Adding comments keeps hardware behavior identical while making the sketch clearer to read.

exercises.prompt: Which of the following is a valid C++ multi-line comment?
exercises.explanation: C++ uses /* ... */ for multi-line comments and // for single-line comments.

exercises.prompt: What is the best use of a comment in an Arduino sketch?
options: Documenting pin wiring, physical units (ms, cm), and why a threshold was chosen.
exercises.explanation: Good comments capture physical context and design reasoning.

summary: Use // for single-line comments and /* ... */ for multi-line blocks.
Document wiring, units, and design intent.
Comments use zero memory on the Arduino.

lessons.title: Variables
lessons.introduction: A variable is a named container in SRAM that stores a value your program can read and update while running.
objectives: Declare, initialize, and update variables in C++.
Follow valid C++ variable naming rules.
Distinguish variable declaration from variable assignment.
conceptExplanation: Sensors change constantly: room brightness rises and falls, robot distance shrinks as you approach a wall, and timers tick upward. Variables give your program a named memory slot in SRAM to hold those changing values.
Always initialize a variable when you create it (e.g., int count = 0;) so it never starts with unpredictable garbage data.
lessons.analogy: A variable is like a labeled storage bin on a workbench: the label stays the same, while the contents inside can be swapped anytime.

syntaxExplanation.summary: Core C++ syntax pattern for Variables:
rules: Names can contain letters, digits, and underscores, but cannot start with a digit.
No spaces or C++ keywords (like int or if) allowed in names.
Use camelCase for variables (e.g., sensorReading, motorSpeed).

codeExamples.title: Tracking a Live Counter Variable
codeExamples.description: Increments a counter variable each second and prints it to Serial Monitor.

lineByLine.explanation: Creates an integer variable initialized to 0.
Reads the current value, adds 1, and stores the result back.
Prints the updated value each second.

lessons.realWorldApplication: Odometry counters on wheeled robots use variables to count encoder ticks and calculate distance traveled.

commonMistakes.mistake: Re-declaring the same variable type inside loop()
commonMistakes.fix: Write 'blinkCount = 5;' to update an existing variable, NOT 'int blinkCount = 5;'.

commonMistakes.mistake: Starting a variable name with a number like 1stSensor
commonMistakes.fix: Start names with a letter: firstSensor or sensor1.

tryItYourself.title: m03_variables.ino
tryItYourself.challengePrompt: Change blinkCount to increase by 2 each cycle instead of 1.
tryItYourself.expectedBehavior: Serial Monitor prints 2, 4, 6, 8... once per second.

exercises.prompt: Which variable name is VALID in C++?
exercises.explanation: Variable names cannot start with a digit, contain spaces, or match reserved keywords.

exercises.prompt: What value is printed?
exercises.explanation: score is overwritten with 25, then increased by 5 to become 30.

summary: Variables store changeable values in SRAM.
Always initialize variables with a starting value.
Use clear camelCase names following C++ identifier rules.

lessons.title: Data Types
lessons.introduction: Choosing the right C++ data type saves precious microcontroller SRAM and prevents integer overflow bugs.
objectives: Compare int, unsigned long, float, bool, and char.
Explain why millis() requires unsigned long instead of int.
Select the smallest safe data type for sensor and timing data.
conceptExplanation: Microcontrollers have limited memory — an Arduino Uno R3 has only 2,048 bytes of SRAM! Every data type uses a specific number of bytes and holds a specific range of values.

On 8-bit AVR boards (Uno R3/Nano Classic/Mega), int is 16-bit (-32,768 to 32,767). That means an int overflows after just 32.7 seconds if you store milliseconds in it! Always use unsigned long (32-bit, up to ~49.7 days) for millis() timestamps.
lessons.analogy: Data types are like shipping boxes: you wouldn't ship a single screw in a refrigerator crate, and you can't fit a refrigerator in an envelope.

syntaxExplanation.summary: Core C++ syntax pattern for Data Types:
syntaxExplanation.pattern: bool (true/false) | char ('A') | int (whole numbers) | unsigned long (timers) | float (decimals)
rules: int on Uno R3 is 16-bit (-32,768 to 32,767); on Uno R4 & ESP32 it is 32-bit.
Use unsigned long for millis() and pulseIn() durations.
Use float for decimals like distance in cm or temperature in Celsius.

codeExamples.title: Choosing Appropriate Arduino Data Types
codeExamples.description: Demonstrates bool, int, unsigned long, and float side by side.

lineByLine.explanation: 1 byte storing true or false.
4 bytes storing positive millisecond timestamps safely.
4 bytes storing decimal measurements.

lessons.realWorldApplication: Preventing int overflow in timers is critical for weather stations and robots that run for hours or days without resetting.

commonMistakes.mistake: Storing millis() in an int
commonMistakes.fix: Always declare timing variables as unsigned long.

commonMistakes.mistake: Using float for simple pin numbers or counters
commonMistakes.fix: Integers are faster and use less Flash/CPU on 8-bit boards.

tryItYourself.title: m03_data_types.ino
tryItYourself.challengePrompt: Add a char variable named grade = 'A'; and print it to Serial Monitor.
tryItYourself.expectedBehavior: Serial Monitor prints 4.95, the startup millisecond count, and the character A.

exercises.prompt: Which data type MUST you use to store values returned by millis()?
exercises.explanation: millis() returns an unsigned long (32-bit unsigned integer); using int overflows in ~32.7 seconds on Uno R3.

exercises.prompt: Declare a decimal variable named tempC initialized to 23.5.
exercises.explanation: float stores floating-point decimal numbers in Arduino C++.

summary: Every C++ variable has a fixed data type and memory size.
Use unsigned long for millis() and pulseIn() timing.
Use float for decimals, bool for true/false, and int for whole numbers.

lessons.title: Constants
lessons.introduction: Constants store fixed values like pin numbers and thresholds so your code cannot accidentally overwrite them.
objectives: Declare read-only constants using const.
Explain why const int is preferred over #define for pin numbers.
Eliminate 'magic numbers' from Arduino sketches.
conceptExplanation: If a motor pin is wired to Digital Pin 5, that number never changes while the robot runs. Marking it const tells the compiler to forbid accidental modification — and often lets the compiler optimize away SRAM usage completely.
Using ALL_CAPS_WITH_UNDERSCORES for constants (like LED_PIN or SAFE_DISTANCE_CM) lets anyone spot fixed configuration values immediately.
lessons.analogy: A constant is like engraving a number into metal instead of writing it on a whiteboard — you can read it forever, but nobody can smudge it.

syntaxExplanation.summary: Core C++ syntax pattern for Constants:
rules: A const variable must be initialized when declared.
Trying to reassign a const causes a helpful compile-time error.
Prefer const over #define because const respects C++ data types and scope.

codeExamples.title: Replacing Magic Numbers with Constants
codeExamples.description: Uses named constants for pins and timing thresholds.

lineByLine.explanation: Locks LED_PIN to 8; changing the wire later only requires editing one line.
Clarifies both purpose and unit (milliseconds).

lessons.realWorldApplication: When migrating a sketch from Arduino Uno to Mega or ESP32, having all pins in a const block at the top makes re-mapping effortless.

commonMistakes.mistake: Trying to change a const inside loop()
commonMistakes.fix: Remove const only if the value genuinely needs to change at runtime.

commonMistakes.mistake: Scattering raw numbers like 8 and 300 across 15 lines
commonMistakes.fix: Centralize configuration values as named constants at the top.

tryItYourself.title: m03_constants.ino
tryItYourself.challengePrompt: Change BLINK_INTERVAL_MS to 150 in one place to speed up both delays.
tryItYourself.expectedBehavior: Editing the single constant updates both ON and OFF timing cleanly.

exercises.prompt: Why will this sketch fail to compile?
options: You cannot assign a new value to a const variable.
const must be written inside loop().
exercises.explanation: const marks a value read-only; the compiler blocks reassignment.

exercises.prompt: Declare a constant float named MAX_VOLTS equal to 5.0.
exercises.explanation: const float MAX_VOLTS = 5.0; creates a typed read-only constant.

summary: Use const for pin numbers, thresholds, and fixed physical constants.
Constants prevent accidental overwrites and eliminate magic numbers.
Name constants in ALL_CAPS for immediate clarity.

lessons.title: Operators
lessons.introduction: Operators perform actions on variables and values — including assignment (=), arithmetic (+, -, *, /, %), and compound shorthands (+=, ++).
objectives: Use assignment (=) and compound assignment (+=, -=) cleanly.
Understand increment (++) and decrement (--).
Apply the modulo (%) operator for cycling patterns.
conceptExplanation: Operators are the verbs of C++. You already used the assignment operator (=) to store values. Compound operators like count += 5; and count++; make loops and counters concise and idiomatic.
The modulo operator (%) returns the remainder of integer division (for example, 7 % 3 is 1). Robotics programmers love % for wrapping an index back to 0 when cycling through LEDs or menu modes.
lessons.analogy: Modulo (%) is like a 12-hour clock: after 12, it wraps cleanly back around instead of counting to 13.

syntaxExplanation.summary: Core C++ syntax pattern for Operators:
rules: = assigns a value; == compares two values (never mix them up!).
++ adds 1; -- subtracts 1.
% only works on integer types, not float.

codeExamples.title: Cycling Modes with Modulo (%)
codeExamples.description: Cycles a mode index 0 -> 1 -> 2 -> 0 cleanly using %.

lineByLine.explanation: Increments mode and wraps 3 cleanly back to 0.

lessons.realWorldApplication: Multi-mode flashlights and robot state selectors use modulo (%) to cycle through modes with a single push button.

commonMistakes.mistake: Using = instead of == in an if statement
commonMistakes.fix: Single = assigns! Use == to check equality.

commonMistakes.mistake: Using % on float variables
commonMistakes.fix: Modulo works only with integers (int, long, byte).

tryItYourself.title: m03_operators.ino
tryItYourself.challengePrompt: Change % 3 to % 4 so the mode cycles 0, 1, 2, 3, 0.
tryItYourself.expectedBehavior: Serial Monitor prints 0, 1, 2, 3 and repeats back to 0.

exercises.prompt: What does 11 % 4 evaluate to?
exercises.explanation: 4 goes into 11 twice (8) with a remainder of 3.

exercises.prompt: Use the shorthand increment operator to add 1 to count.
exercises.explanation: count++; increments count by 1.

summary: Assignment (=) stores values; compound operators (+=, ++) update them concisely.
Modulo (%) returns integer remainder and is ideal for wrap-around cycles.
Never confuse assignment (=) with equality comparison (==).

lessons.title: Arithmetic Expressions
lessons.introduction: Arithmetic expressions combine numbers, variables, and math operators to convert raw sensor numbers into real-world engineering units.
objectives: Apply C++ operator precedence (parentheses, *, /, %, then +, -).
Avoid integer division truncation when computing decimals.
Convert raw ADC readings into voltage.
conceptExplanation: C++ follows standard math precedence: multiplication and division happen before addition and subtraction, and parentheses ( ) always run first.
Watch out for integer division! In C++, 5 / 2 evaluates to 2 (the .5 is chopped off) because both numbers are integers. Writing 5.0 / 2.0 produces 2.5.
lessons.analogy: Integer division is like counting how many full 2-liter bottles you can fill from 5 liters of water: you get 2 full bottles, and the leftover half is ignored unless you use decimal floats.

syntaxExplanation.summary: Core C++ syntax pattern for Arithmetic Expressions:
rules: Use parentheses to make order of operations unmistakable.
Include .0 on constants (e.g., 5.0, 1023.0) when you want a decimal result.

codeExamples.title: Converting Raw ADC to Voltage
codeExamples.description: Converts a 10-bit Uno R3 analog reading into volts.

lineByLine.explanation: Mid-scale 10-bit ADC reading.
Uses 5.0 and 1023.0 so C++ performs floating-point division (~2.50 V).
Prints the float rounded to 2 decimal places.

lessons.realWorldApplication: Ultrasonic distance meters, battery voltage monitors, and thermistor thermometers all rely on accurate floating-point arithmetic expressions.

commonMistakes.mistake: Writing 5 / 1023 instead of 5.0 / 1023.0
commonMistakes.fix: Integer 5 / 1023 evaluates to 0! Always include .0 for floating-point math.

commonMistakes.mistake: Skipping parentheses in complex formulas
commonMistakes.fix: Parentheses eliminate precedence bugs and improve clarity.

tryItYourself.challengePrompt: Change 5.0 to 3.3 and 1023.0 to 4095.0 to match an ESP32 12-bit ADC formula.
tryItYourself.expectedBehavior: Prints the scaled voltage with two decimal places in Serial Monitor.

exercises.prompt: What value is stored in result?
exercises.explanation: Both 7 and 2 are integers, so C++ performs integer division and drops the fractional remainder.

exercises.prompt: Which expression computes the average of a and b accurately as a float?
exercises.explanation: Parentheses ensure addition happens first, and 2.0 forces floating-point division.

summary: Parentheses control arithmetic precedence cleanly.
Integer division truncates decimals — use .0 literals for floating-point results.
Use arithmetic expressions to turn raw ADC values into physical units.

lessons.title: Comparison Operators
lessons.introduction: Comparison operators compare two values and produce a boolean result: true or false.
objectives: Use all six comparison operators: ==, !=, <, <=, >, >=.
Explain the critical difference between = and ==.
Write sensor threshold comparisons accurately.
conceptExplanation: Every decision your Arduino makes starts with a comparison: Is distance less than 20 cm? Is temperature greater than or equal to 30 C? Is the button state equal to LOW?
All six comparison operators evaluate to a bool (true or false), which feeds directly into if statements and loops.
lessons.analogy: Comparison operators are like a balance scale that answers a single yes-or-no question about two weights.

syntaxExplanation.summary: Core C++ syntax pattern for Comparison Operators:
rules: Always use DOUBLE equals (==) to test equality.
!= means 'not equal to'.

codeExamples.title: Comparing Sensor Readings
codeExamples.description: Evaluates threshold comparisons and prints boolean results (1 = true, 0 = false).

lineByLine.explanation: Evaluates to true because 320 is less than 400.
Tests equality without changing lightVal.

lessons.realWorldApplication: Thermostats, automatic streetlights, and obstacle detectors all depend on comparison operators to react to sensor thresholds.

commonMistakes.mistake: Writing if (x = 5) instead of if (x == 5)
commonMistakes.fix: Single = overwrites x with 5 and evaluates true! Always double-check ==.

commonMistakes.mistake: Off-by-one boundary (< vs <=)
commonMistakes.fix: Decide explicitly whether the exact threshold value should trigger the action.

tryItYourself.title: m03_comparisons.ino
tryItYourself.challengePrompt: Change lightVal to 400 and test the difference between < 400 and <= 400.
tryItYourself.expectedBehavior: At 400, lightVal < 400 prints 0 (false), while lightVal <= 400 prints 1 (true).

exercises.prompt: Which operator tests whether two values are NOT equal?
exercises.explanation: In C++, != checks inequality.

exercises.prompt: What bug is hidden in this if condition?
options: It uses assignment (=) instead of equality comparison (==).
LOW cannot be compared to buttonState.
exercises.explanation: Single = assigns LOW (0) to buttonState instead of comparing them.

summary: Six comparison operators (==, !=, <, <=, >, >=) return true or false.
Never confuse = (assignment) with == (equality).
Check boundary conditions (< vs <=) carefully.

lessons.title: Logical Operators
lessons.introduction: Logical operators combine or invert boolean conditions: AND (&&), OR (||), and NOT (!).
objectives: Build compound conditions using &&, ||, and !.
Evaluate truth tables for AND, OR, and NOT.
Use ! to toggle boolean states cleanly.
conceptExplanation: Real robots rarely make decisions from just one sensor. Logical AND (&&) is true only when BOTH sides are true. Logical OR (||) is true when AT LEAST ONE side is true. Logical NOT (!) flips true to false and false to true.
You will also see ! used constantly to toggle an LED: ledState = !ledState;.
lessons.analogy: AND (&&) is two switches wired in series — both must be closed for current to flow. OR (||) is two switches wired in parallel — closing either one lights the bulb.

syntaxExplanation.summary: Core C++ syntax pattern for Logical Operators:
syntaxExplanation.pattern:
condA && condB   // AND
condA || condB   // OR
!condA           // NOT
rules: Use double && and double || for logical tests (single & and | are bitwise operators).
Parenthesize mixed && and || expressions for clarity.

codeExamples.title: Safe Range Check with &&
codeExamples.description: Verifies a sensor value sits inside a valid operating window.

lineByLine.explanation: Both lower and upper bounds must be satisfied simultaneously.

lessons.realWorldApplication: Battery chargers use && to allow charging only when voltage is below max AND battery temperature is within safe limits.

commonMistakes.mistake: Writing 18 <= tempC <= 26 (invalid chained math in C++)
commonMistakes.fix: Always split range checks into two comparisons joined by &&: (tempC >= 18 && tempC <= 26).

commonMistakes.mistake: Using single & instead of &&
commonMistakes.fix: Use && for boolean logic.

tryItYourself.title: m03_logical.ino
tryItYourself.challengePrompt: Change tempC to 30 and observe the output.
tryItYourself.expectedBehavior: At 30, Serial Monitor prints OUT OF RANGE.

exercises.prompt: How do you correctly check if x is between 10 and 20 inclusive in C++?
exercises.explanation: C++ requires two separate comparisons connected by &&.

exercises.prompt: If bool active = false; what is !active?
exercises.explanation: The NOT operator (!) inverts false to true.

summary: && requires both conditions true; || requires at least one true; ! inverts a boolean.
Always write range checks as (x >= min && x <= max).
Use !flag to toggle boolean states cleanly.

lessons.title: Type Conversion
lessons.introduction: Type conversion (casting) explicitly converts a value from one C++ data type to another so math and hardware outputs stay accurate.
objectives: Distinguish implicit conversion from explicit casting.
Use explicit float casting to prevent integer division loss.
Understand truncation when converting float to int.
conceptExplanation: Sometimes you have two int variables (like totalDistance and sampleCount) and you need their decimal average. If you write totalDistance / sampleCount, C++ performs integer division and drops the remainder.

Casting one operand to float — (float)totalDistance / sampleCount — forces floating-point division. Conversely, casting a float like 24.9 to int truncates it to 24 (it chops off .9 rather than rounding!).
lessons.analogy: Casting a float to an int is like reading only the whole dollars on a $24.99 price tag — the cents are dropped, not rounded up.

syntaxExplanation.summary: Core C++ syntax pattern for Type Conversion:
syntaxExplanation.pattern:
float avg = (float)sum / count;
int whole = (int)3.9; // becomes 3
rules: Casting float -> int truncates toward zero; use round() if you want rounding.
Cast before dividing, not after: (float)(5 / 2) is still 2.0!

codeExamples.title: Explicit Float Cast for Sensor Averaging
codeExamples.description: Computes an accurate decimal average from integer sensor readings.

lineByLine.explanation: Divides two ints first (3), then stores 3.00.
Converts sum to 15.0 first, yielding 3.75.

lessons.realWorldApplication: Sensor smoothing filters average integer ADC samples; explicit float casting preserves precision before feeding PID controllers.

commonMistakes.mistake: Casting too late: (float)(sum / samples)
commonMistakes.fix: The division inside parentheses already truncated! Cast one operand before dividing.

commonMistakes.mistake: Assuming (int)2.9 rounds to 3
commonMistakes.fix: It truncates to 2; use round(2.9) when rounding is desired.

tryItYourself.title: m03_casting.ino
tryItYourself.challengePrompt: Change sum to 23 and samples to 4 and compare wrongAvg vs rightAvg.
tryItYourself.expectedBehavior: Serial Monitor prints 5 for integer division and 5.75 for float-cast division.

exercises.prompt: What value does (int)9.95 produce in C++?
exercises.explanation: Casting a float to int truncates the fractional part without rounding.

exercises.prompt: Which line prevents integer division truncation when a and b are int?
exercises.explanation: Casting 'a' before division forces floating-point arithmetic.

summary: Explicit casting converts one data type to another intentionally.
Cast an operand to float BEFORE dividing two integers.
Casting float to int truncates rather than rounds.
